utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic know as Vlado.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we move on to our next witness, may I discuss a few housekeeping matters? First of all, let me tell you that I have already written and signed and even filed a request to the President of our Tribunal concerning the visit to Ahmici. You will find it in a few hours, because it's being processed by the Registry. Informally she is agreeable, but, of course -- when I got in touch with her she said she was agreeable, but, of course, she and the Registrar will have to look at the financial and security implications. Now, if money is available and the security problems are sorted out, we will have to propose something specific to the Registrar, and so, therefore -- about practical arrangements. I wonder if we could know from the Defence and Prosecution how many members of the two teams are prepared and willing to go to Ahmici, and in particular, as far as the Defence is concerned, whether they would leave from here, The Hague, with the whole team, or whether they prefer to go there from Croatia. So I wonder whether Mr. Pavkovic could kindly get in touch with Mr. Terrier later on today or Monday to sort out all these practical arrangements and make a proposal to the Registrar, or to the Court about the practical side of this matter. I see Mr. Pavkovic would like to say a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Really, we will meet with the Prosecution after we have, ourselves, coordinated the matter, and we will inform you duly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavkovic. Now, the second point relates to the list of Defence witnesses filed, by counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic, a few days ago. I wonder whether the Prosecution are prepared to tell us now about their reaction to that list, whether they intend also to call also some of the ten witnesses the Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic proposes to call. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. On that list of witnesses which was submitted to us by the Defence for Vlatko Kupreskic, we do not have any intention to call any of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, the third point, I gather that the Prosecution have requested the postponement of Mr. Akhavan's cross-examination. We have to accept this postponement somewhat reluctantly, because, of course, it's more efficient and judicially economical to have the cross-examination after the examination. But as the Romans used to say, "Ad impossibilia nemo tenetur," so nobody is duty-bound to something which that is totally impossible. However, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Defence for kindly accepting this postponement. I understand Mr. Akhavan will come here on Monday. Now, the final point is about the witnesses for next week. You know, so far we, in the Court, we have received the various witness statements in dribs and drabs, and I've been trying to have a list of their statements, as well as the actual text of the statements. I wonder whether the Prosecution could be so kind as to give us a sort of consolidated list of at least the dates of the various statements made by each witness, because I am a bit mystified about the -- how many statements have been made by each witness. In one case I counted almost five or six. I mean, in the case of Witness 8. I don't know whether we can mention that name, number 8 in the last -- is he a protected witness, number 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. So number 8, a lot of statements. So if we could get a list -- at least a list of their statements with the dates when they were made. I have prepared my own list but I am not sure whether it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will make an effort to submit those documents. Please understand that not all of these witness statements were taken in the same manner by the same authorities, and nor are all related to the same proceedings. Some statements, for example, for Witness number 7 on that list, was recorded on videotape and that was a transcript that was submitted, of course, to the Defence. So sometimes you must understand it is difficult to submit that kind of list, but we will make an effort to do so, nonetheless, this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I think it will be useful to receive that list as soon as possible, because the weather here at The Hague is conducive to much work even over the weekend. So we can take advantage, at least, of the bad weather. Final point, and here, of course, I don't want to interfere with the discretionary power of the Prosecution to decide upon their own strategy concerning the order of appearance of witnesses, but I was wondering whether, having read carefully, I think, the statements of -- nine, the next witnesses for next week, I was wondering whether there's a particular reason why you have, for instance, separated number 7 from number 10. If I am not wrong, they deal with the same episode and might prove useful for the Court to hear these witnesses one after the other, As for number 8, of course, this is going to be a crucial witness, and I wonder whether you realistically plan to call him next week, because judging from the pace of our proceedings, it is likely that this would be put off until after the break, the one-week break. But as I say, it is for you. We fully respect your discretionary power, your right to decide upon the order. But just to make our proceedings more efficient, and also to get a better picture, I thought you might wish to reconsider the order in which you intend to call those witnesses. For instance, I take the liberty of humbly suggesting that, for instance, number 8 might be brought forward so that we know whether he will be heard next week or after the break, and then number 7 and number 10 could be put together. It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, indeed, we will reflect on the issue you've just raised. Nonetheless, I would like to remind the Court that sometimes we might deal with very difficult logistical matters. These people are coming from far away, and sometimes we must follow these wishes they express, which are legitimate, and we must try to satisfy these wishes, and which means that at times, indeed, and we have spoken with this Tribunal about this matter in the beginning of this trial, that at times we'll be required to interrupt some of the logical order in which these witnesses may appear. We regret this will be the case, but sometimes we cannot do otherwise. Today, indeed, I do share your sentiments and sentiments of the court. I believe that there is a legitimate observation made, that the examination-in-chief of Mr. Akhavan and -- the cross-examination, rather, be postponed until Monday. I think, yes, indeed, that is something that shows the flexibility of the Defence. It shows also the proper conduct of the proceedings here before this Tribunal. We are thankful for that, but we hope that this mix up in the order of witnesses does not present itself again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now then proceed to the testimony of witness number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Here again, I see -- I imagine we will not have the possibility of having cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It will be ideal, yes, indeed, Your Honour, it would be ideal to have it at the same time. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning Witness E. Could you please read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Microphone. There's no microphone. There was no translation. Could you please repeat your declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no sound coming. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There is no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, still no sound coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May we consider that -- but on the other hand there must be, afterwards, a translation, otherwise we could move forward. Mr. Terrier, were you able to receive anything in French? Was there a French interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Shall we try again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Show it to the witness. I'm sorry. Please go ahead. Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you are a protected witness in this courtroom. Therefore, you may express yourself as you wish in serenity, with no fear whatsoever. All I ask is that you do not state any names, and that you not give any identifying information about yourself or your family unless we go into closed session, in which case that may be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You can't hear. Even on 7?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I was simply stating that you are here as a protected witness. You're benefiting from protective measures, and that your identity will not be known outside of this courtroom. Therefore, you may express yourself with serenity and fully. I simply would like to ask that during the course of your testimony that no names, nor any information which may identify yourself or your family be made. We are asking if we need information of this type, then we will go into closed session to obtain that type of information. Witness, could you please indicate to us what your -- your age and the age that you had in the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: In early 1993, I was 15 years old, and now I'm 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the interpreters do not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is on, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please describe the composition of your family? Mr. President, I did not receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, would you please repeat your question, because perhaps now the system is working and the interpretation into French may be working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please tell us what the composition of your family was in early 1993, without giving any names, of course.

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: My father, my mother, my sister and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your sister in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: In 1993 she was 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what area or city are you originally from?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: From Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what date and for what reason did you arrive in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Between 20th and 25 November. We came to Ahmici because we were expelled from the place where we lived by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We would like to submit to the witness an aerial photo. This will show the neighbourhood -- this will enable the witness to indicate in which neighbourhood he was living in Ahmici in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Registrar has rightly pointed out that we should probably go into closed session now because of the picture, the photograph you're going to show. So we go into closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor just asked the witness to identify the -- his house on the basis of the aerial photograph. I personally believe that to make such identification on the basis of a house already encircled on a photograph does not really constitute a real identification. It is simply showing a location that the witness is advised ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, this is an indication made by the witness of where he was living. I believe it is indisputable that it is the house which he was living in with his family. I do not believe that there is any real question in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I agree with the Prosecutor. It is not in dispute. If you start objecting even to minor things, such as the photograph and the picture of the house where he was living, then the trial will end maybe in two years' time. This is really a question which is not in dispute. If you have any objection on the merits, then you can put your objection to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with you with respect to this witness. He did live in this house. However, I have noticed that on a number of aerial photographs which were shown to other witnesses previously where it was very crucial that a witness recognises or identifies it, they were already pre-marked. So in this particular case, I agree with you. But in principle, I disagree with the method where the witness is shown pre-marked photographs. As far as this particular photograph is concerned, we really can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. But also in future, as I say, if the Prosecutor prefers to present pre-marked photographs with a circle around a house, you are most welcome to object if you find that the indication of that house is in dispute, if you dispute the indication of that house. But as far as the method, the approach is concerned, I don't think it is questionable. Let us leave it for the future. You may proceed, Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe there are no objections with regards that witness and the indication made by the witness as to the location of his house. I would also like to make an observation that the circle is fairly large, and within that circle, there are several houses, and that the witness indicated or pointed out one of the houses within that circle marked 1. I would like to continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the day of the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to this Court the days that preceded the attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, I was in the house almost the whole day. I was watching television, Busovaca TV, and there was some kind of a parade of the Croatian army. I did not pay that much attention to it, but I recall a detail. It was a commander, whom I did not know, and he said, "Tomorrow, we are going to attack Jajce," even though we all knew that Jajce had fallen about two or three months earlier, sometime in October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jajce fell into the hands of the forces in the western part of Bosnia, above Travnik, and it fell into which hands?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: It fell to the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what you heard on television reports about the war against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I don't know that. But we all knew that at that time, it was very difficult given the numbers of them at that parade. It was incomprehensible, almost, to see all these people going to Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please go back to what you recall about the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes. On 16 April, 1993, at 5.50, we were awakened by shooting. We got up. I was the first to get up and open the window in the hallway of the house. I saw two soldiers in front of our house, that is, the house where we were staying, who were standing near the house of Husein Ahmic, and they called him out and they ordered him to stand against a wall. I closed the window and returned to my family and told them that these HVO soldiers had passed over our house, that we could not go out, that we had to wait to see what would happen next. We waited in the bedroom until ten past six. You could hear the soldiers walking about. There were some bars on our windows. First we heard a kick and then, with their rifle butts, they smashed the windows, and I told my family that we should go because they would throw in a hand grenade. So we went to the kitchen, and as I was closing the door, a hand grenade exploded in the room. I told them to move to the hallway, and as we went there, the second hand grenade exploded in the kitchen. Then we knew that we had to leave there. My mother went out first, followed by my sister, my father, and then I came out of the house last. As soon as we came out, there was a fence at the end of the property, and just on the other side of the fence, we saw two dead bodies. There were two soldiers who were on the road in front of our house, about 10 metres away. They told us, "Hands up and bow your heads and run uphill." We started walking towards them. My father was the last. He was the fourth. However, two additional soldiers stood at the corner of the house, to the right of us, and one of them said, "You, the tall one. Come over here." The three of us, my mother, my sister, and myself went towards the two soldiers who were standing on the road. As we were passing them, I saw two additional dead bodies there. I turned around and my sister also turned around to see where my father was going, and the soldier who was on the road said, "Don't turn around. Keep going. Keep moving." I sort of showed with my head to my sister that she should run. I also turned around once, and I saw my father walking with his hands up. He was walking towards them. The same soldier who was on the road, who had already told us not to turn around, said again, "Don't turn around." I saw that my mother couldn't walk, she was too excited, and I helped her. We moved away maybe 10, 15 metres away from the soldiers, and we heard shots. We did not dare turn around. I did not know whether they had killed my father or whether they had killed the landlord with whom we were staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I must interrupt you one moment and ask for a number of clarifications at this time about what you stated. With regards to those two soldiers that you saw from your window, the window of your house and who were stopping the person who you named as Husein Ahmic, can you please describe how those two soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Camouflage uniforms, multi-coloured, automatic rifles. They had anti-tank rocket launchers which they carried over their shoulders, slung. So that is the description of the ones who were in front of his house. That is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they wearing any masks or were their faces painted?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: They had their backs turned to me, and this is why I saw that they had this anti-tank rocket launchers, and I could not see them because I just gave them sort of a cursory look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that these two soldiers stopped your neighbour, Husein Ahmic. Would you please explain what happened later?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: They were in front of the house, and they called him out, said, "The old one, come out." And his wife said, "Please don't. Don't. He's an elderly man." However, they did not respond to that. I saw that he walked past them along the wall. It was some kind of a shed or garage, and he was against that wall. I could not see whether they killed him or not because I could not see it from the window, but I recall them putting him against a wall. I don't know what happened after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him again after that time, Mr. Husein Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No, we never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how Mr. Husein Ahmic was dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: He had on a pair of trousers and shoes, and now I cannot recall -- there was a shirt. I don't know whether he had a jacket on or whether he carried it over his arm. That, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No. The man was somewhere between 55 and 60 years of age. He was an elderly man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let us now talk about the two soldiers you saw on the road at the time you left your house with your family. You indicated that two soldiers stopped you and they asked you to raise your hands. Do you remember how these two soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I do remember. The two soldiers who stopped us on the road, one of them was wearing a mask. You could only see his eyes and mouth. The other one had his face painted in black. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and they had automatic rifles on the left -- maybe I'm wrong. But in any event, they did have insignia of the military police which are usually placed on the left or right arm, I don't know. But at any rate, they had the military police insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the faces of these soldiers, or at least the soldier who was not wearing any type of mask?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: The one who did not have a mask, because his face was really painted fully, so I could not recognise him, but I described him as somebody who was lean and his height was somewhere between 1.80 to 1.85 metres, he had somewhat receding hair and he parted it to the side and that's all I remember. I have no further description of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you feel that you knew this person, that soldier?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldier you just described, did you have the feeling that you knew him, that you recognised him? Was his face familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I could not tell you because his face was really painted. It's more his height and his being very lanky and his hair, but the face itself I could not recognise because it was all painted in black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some of his physical appearances were familiar to you. What did that tell you?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Perhaps I had seen this person once or twice, but there were a lot of persons who looked alike, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had the feeling that you had already seen that person before. Can you please tell this Court where you felt you had seen that person before? In what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Well, this person that I have just described, I went to the Sutre shop cellar twice, three times, and there I met a similar person. Whether this person was working there in that cellar or not, I really cannot tell, because I would not go there very frequently. I would also go in there for just a short time to buy cigarettes, to buy some provisions like oil or sugar, for a very short time anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the store which is located -- the store called Sutre. Can you please describe it for us? What did the inside of that store look like? How did it look at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I cannot tell you specifically the size, the dimensions, but it was about ten times ten or twelve metres, it looked like it had two, two and a half metre high walls, it had a storeroom, it had a ceiling on top. Inside, there were pallets with provisions like flour, and I presume there was cooking oil, sugar there. Then there was a counter, and behind the counter, there were shelves on which you could see bottles of alcohol or cooking oil or provisions. This is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the owner of that shop?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: The owner was Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person who you're referring to, when you saw him in that store, what was he doing? Was that person there as a client or for something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an objection to raise. The witness had already stated that he did not know whether this person was working there or not. He said that he saw in the shop a similar-looking person, but he did not know whether this person was working there or not, and I really do not see why he is repeating this question to which actually the witness already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I think, judging from the transcript, I think the question put by the Prosecutor was whether the witness knew who was the owner of that shop, and then he said the person you are referring to, when you saw him in that store, what was he doing? He's speaking of the owner of the shop. So probably -- yes. Thank you. You may go on, Mr. Terrier. There was probably a problem of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember, after your arrival in The Hague, whether a number of photographs were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a photo album representing various persons of the male sex all around the same age, and in all, there were some 24 photographs?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you recognised no one in this album?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No, I recognised no one on these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, to completely keep this Court informed, we have a record of the statements made by this witness, information which he will repeat here during his testimony. We have the album of these 24 photographs, and among these 24 photographs, there are two of the accused. The witness recognised none of the persons in this photograph album. We would like to make this clear immediately and inform the Defence under Rule 68. I would also like to attach to the case file before this Court, unless there is an objection from the Defence -- I don't believe there would be an objection -- the written statement signed by the witness during this operation which took place on the 17th of August, and attached to this statement, we have a photocopy -- you may also have the original, if you wish -- but there is the series of photographs which we showed so that this Tribunal will have a very clear idea of how this operation was carried out. I would then ask the usher ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were not able to see what the Prosecutor would like to submit as evidence. We were only provided with a very short notice consisting of one sentence; therefore, we really do not know what is included in this statement and, hence, do not consider this to be admissible as evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why don't you first take a look? Let us leave then this question of admissibility in abeyance, and then after you have had the opportunity to take a look at this statement, you will let us know whether or not you still object. Judging from what Mr. Terrier said a few seconds ago, I think it would be quite admissible, but let us put it off until a bit later. All right. Mr. Terrier, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With the authorisation of this Tribunal, I would like to request the witness to do the following: We know from experience that it is at times difficult to recognise someone on a photograph, but that when one is in the physical presence of that person, the conditions may be different and one's memory may be better at that time. I know that the witness was 15 years of age at that time. I also know very well that the witness has lived for a maximum of five months in Ahmici and that five years has gone by. Nonetheless, I feel that it is necessary to ask this witness to determine whether or not, in this courtroom, he is able to recognise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. If there is an application of this sort, it must be made to the Court, and for myself, I would wish to consider it very carefully in the circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is what Mr. Terrier was going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be. It may be. But I would find it helpful to know, before we go to this, what it is proposed that the witness is going to say about the evidence, and I would propose that he completes his evidence and then we consider this question of further identification so that we know what the background is against which any identification is purported to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Indeed, I was going to request leave of this Court to have this done because perhaps this has been an unusual procedure to carry out and perhaps the Court might reflect on that proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like now to ask you a number of questions regarding the third group of soldiers which you saw near your house; you stated that there were soldiers near the corner of your house. Would you please describe them?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: The description, on the basis of a very brief glimpse of them, would be the following: One of them had a mask with only eyes open, another one was painted with black paint on his face, they were wearing camouflage uniforms, they had automatic machine rifles, and that's all I could see because, as I said before, the other guys, the other two soldiers, would not let us turn around, so I was not allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your father again later?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Since that very day, the 16th of April, 6.15 hours, until today, I never learned about the fate of my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No one indicated to you, for example, where he was buried?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Nobody told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would now request that we return to the time at which you were separated from your father. May we please show the aerial photograph, which I believe is Prosecution Exhibit 98? I do not believe it is necessary that we go back into closed session because the information which I am going to ask him now will not reveal his identity. Witness, would you please look at this aerial photograph? When we met before this hearing, I asked that you indicate for me what path you took with your mother and your sister on this photograph, after your separation from your father, during the course of that day, and you drew out that path. Is that indeed the path which is indicated with a white line on this aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the track.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please then tell us what this path was?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The path that you followed with your mother and sister, it is indicated, as you just stated, on this photograph. Can you please explain to us where you went, what type of path you took?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that. The path we were going along from the house where we resided to this point and from here onward we were accompanied by the two soldiers that were on the road. They could see us as far as this house here. We passed by this house, and then there was some brushes. We had to walk slowly because shooting could be heard here on this site under Roman II. We had to walk the slowest, because there was severe shooting that we could hear and observe from both our left-hand side and our right-hand side. We, I repeat again, were walking very slowly until we arrived at Kermo's house. Here we stayed about 30 minutes or an hour perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you talked about the gunfire or, rather, the fire which was coming to your direction from the left and from the right, could you please indicate exactly where that was?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: When we were walking along this path here encircled and marked with Roman II, this is the way we were walking along. It is from this side, that is from our left-hand side. As we were moving upward, we noticed shots being fired. Actually, there were shots fired from the lower side as well, from the road Zenica/Vitez. And also from this hill as well but I don't know the name of this feature. I know, however, that an 84 machine gun and a sniper were located here on this hill. I saw this very clearly, because it's not that far. Once I arrived in Upper Ahmici, I could see it, because it's only about 200, 250 metres airline, and I could see very well what was located there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that the gunfire was coming from several directions. You indicated, with your pointer, the hill from which fire was coming in your direction. Would you please indicate, in the same way, from which other directions you saw fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: From this direction. However, I couldn't see it. I heard fire coming from this direction, because this part up here, encircled part, is a little lower than the lower part where the shots were fired from. However, it's not very far away; therefore, you could hear shots being fired. There's only perhaps a hundred, a hundred and fifty metres distance here, not more than that. So from this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please indicate the direction? You indicated this on the aerial photograph. Would you please point that out for us? Could you please give it a name?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I cannot give you a name. I can only tell you the houses and the owners of the houses in this area. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to who do they belong?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: One of these houses here belonged to Vlatko Kupreskic. The others, I don't know, because let me recall that I wasn't living there for a long time, and I don't know the owners of the other houses who were of Croatian ethnicity. I just know that his house was located here, because it is a big and very solid house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Upper Ahmici, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: When we arrived in Upper Ahmici, we stayed there in a house from about 10.30 p.m. At that time, from other houses, from the summer houses, people would come and gather. So a group of women and children would gather there. So those who survived of the men as well would come and gather here. Then the group headed towards the village of Vhrovine and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, subject to that issue with regards to the identification of some of the accused, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have decided not to grant the request of the Prosecutor. In this particular case, we think that “dock identification” is not appropriate. So, therefore, we may now move on to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I request that Prosecution Exhibits 97 and 98 be tendered, and, of course, we still have to suspend the issue of document 99. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic, could you be so kind as to let us know who is going to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can inform you that the witness will be examined by our colleague Madam Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, followed by Mr. Radovic, in closing, Defence counsel Braislav Krajina. Just one correction. The first witness is going to be examined by Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Radovic? Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when exactly did you come to The Hague, just now before this trial?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Several days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Not much time has elapsed. Could you give us a precise day, please? Did you arrive prior to 17 August? Can you tell us how many days? (No audible answer) I'm sorry, the witness has only nodded, which cannot be taken down. Could you please give us verbal answers?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I arrived before 17 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: How many days before 17 August?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Couple of days before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in The Hague, how many days prior to 17 August did you first get in touch with the investigators of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: When I arrived, I had contact on the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that first day when you had contact with the Tribunal investigators, did you sign anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No, I did not sign anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any contact on the following days?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Not the very next day, but I did have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any additional contacts before 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the first contact, what did the contact consist of? Did you give any statements or did you just discuss weather in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: We talked about my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: About the statement which I'd given, whether I had misstated something, whether I had omitted anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something in that regard. Did the investigator point out anything that you may have misstated?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: When I had given that statement, I did not believe that I had misstated anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So in which direction did this conversation go regarding whether you'd misstated anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Could you point out to us, to the court, the relevance. Tell us what the relevance of your questions is. To what extent what you are asking is relevant to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutor requested that the witness statement be entered into evidence. We believe that this witness was influenced to identify one of the accused, and since the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. If you read this statement, you will see that at the end the witness clearly states that he is unable to identify any of the 20 photographs. So he does not recognise anybody. I don't see why you are putting all these questions, because this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I know. Just to show that an attempt was made to influence this witness to make an identification, but if you believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Move on to other questions, please. This is not acceptable. It is clearly inconsistent with what the Prosecutor did with this document, in producing this document, which shows that the Prosecutor did not attempt to influence the witness, and this is the clear evidence. Please move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have just a small, brief comment to make. I understand the difficulties that the Defence has in this particular issue. We both come from different systems than the ones used by this court. We both come from very similar systems, in fact. In fact, in our own systems it is completely unusual, and sometimes forbidden, for a witness to meet with the counsel ahead of time, particularly with regards to witnesses for either parties. But in this case, the Defence, I hope, will understand that indeed when the witness comes to The Hague, we go over the witness's testimony, we sometimes submit to this witness photographs, which, of course, about which we will be able to discuss in court. But it should be understood, and I hope that Mr. Radovic understands and does not put into question the morality of the Prosecution. He should understand that we are not trying to influence this witness's testimony. We understand that the witness is testifying under oath, and we are here to look for the complete truth. We simply wish to know what occurred and we wish to cover the facts and this is how we proceed. And, Mr. Radovic, I hope you understand this and do not be surprised if each witness will have already been met with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor beforehand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Terrier, for reminding this court that indeed, and as you stated, the legal traditions of the various parties may indeed change the approach one may have. And I do indeed share of view of Mr. Terrier that since you come from a country in which you have a civil law tradition, such as in Croatia, in France, in Germany and the former Yugoslavia, I understand that the approach would be very different, and in that case one might be very surprised about what one sees here. Nonetheless, Mr. Radovic, please understand that as Mr. Terrier has underlined, rightly so, that you are in a different legal framework today, and so you must please try to adapt to this new framework. You are now working in a system which is not a civil law system as we are used to practising in our own respective countries. In this case, the procedures do indeed allow for contact between the Prosecution and witness, and this also goes for the Defence. This is the principle of the equality of arms which comes into play here, so this gives this right to the Prosecutor. So we will indeed have witnesses here, witnesses from the Defence, in which you yourself will have the same rights, the rights to interview the witnesses for the Defence beforehand. What the Prosecutor has done in this particular case, in fact, they wrote this document, this shows that they have acted in good faith and in a very professional manner. Therefore, I think one should take note of that particular attitude, and I also would be appreciative if you would move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have become familiar with the rules. Mr. President, again let me repeat. We are familiar with the rules regarding this procedure, and we know that the Prosecution has the right to talk to the witnesses, as we do. And we realise and appreciate that the procedure here is different from the, let's say, Germanic type of procedure to which we are used. However, we believe that not all the statements which the Prosecution has taken of witnesses have been provided to us, or at least not in a timely manner. This particular statement bears the date of 17 August. It was only provided to us today, just prior to this witness's testimony. So we had no opportunity to study it, and now we are asked to say whether we agree that it is -- whether we had any objections to this statement. We would just like to make sure that there are no other written statements of their -- or records of their conversations, but we would like to stick to the rules that guide this Tribunal, and if you allow me, I will go on with my questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you were a displaced person and that you came to Vitez as a displaced person. Do you know, were there many displaced persons, Bosniaks, in that area?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I don't know, but they were from different areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which areas did they come?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: They came from Jajce. They were from Krajina, from Jajce, from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately the number of the expelled Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a displaced person or refugee, did you receive any assistance in -- such as in clothing, food and other items?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Merhamet means?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any assistance through Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: In a span of four months we received ten kilograms of flour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally go to collect that assistance?

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a closed session Your Honours, or is it open? Very well, then you don't need to tell me who went to collect it. Please don't tell me the name, just "father," "mother," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Witness E.
utterances.text: It was my mother who went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. I think Mrs. Glumac is next.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it possible for me to do the examination in one go or if we're going to make a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we'll resume at twenty-five past eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, will you allow me to say a few words because, having looked at the transcript, it seems that Mr. Radovic put into question the way in which the Prosecutor and the Office of the Prosecutor has proceeded with the witness which we are now hearing. I would simply like to state and to remind the Defence in particular that the interview was on the 17th of August that we had with this witness and that immediately thereafter, we sent a notice to the Defence, based on Rule 68 of the Rules, indicating that there was exculpatory evidence, and this notice was, of course, signed for and given on the 19th of August to a representative of the Defence, and indeed today we produced that document which we then submitted to the Tribunal, and so we would prefer this also be entered into evidence. So on the 19th of August, the Defence knew that the witness had been shown the photographs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. To avoid any loss of time, Mr. Radovic, you may make a few brief remarks, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I can only confirm that we have received this from the OTP. We have, however, not received the supplementary minutes or statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Probably, at the end of this hearing, you will be able to state whether or not you are objecting to the admission of this document into evidence. I would like now to ask Mrs. Glumac to start cross-examining the witness. However, we have no witness. (The witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would request Your Honour to go into closed session because we will try to identify the location, the site, and the houses in this area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We are now in closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 11.56 a.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of August, 1998, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
